title: The fear of death
hook: no one who fears death can be free

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was choose: judge before the friendship, trust after it. Your line was speak as boldly with them as with yourself.
screen: `SPEAK AS BOLDLY WITH THEM AS WITH YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: A small child can be terrified of the dark hallway, the thing under the bed, the shadow on the wall. Grown-ups smile, because they know what's really there. Seneca, in his fourth letter, suggests grown-ups aren't finished with that kind of fear. They've only traded the hallway for bigger things. One fear he names directly is death. This is a serious day, so we'll take it gently, and only as far as the letter goes.
screen: `A CHILD AFRAID OF THE DARK.` → `GROWN-UPS HAVE BIGGER FEARS.` → `THE FEAR OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Leaving boyhood behind is one thing, Seneca tells Lucilius, but leaving behind a child's fears is another. Many grown people still carry the frights of the nursery, only now they're afraid of bigger things. He describes people clinging to life the way someone swept along by a flooding river grabs at thorns and brambles on the bank. Holding on so hard, they can't actually live. No one, he says, can have a peaceful life who thinks too much about lengthening it. He's blunt about what Romans of his day knew. Great generals had been killed by a boy king's servants, by enemies, by their own emperor's order. Power doesn't buy safety. Then a sharp line: whoever cares nothing for his own life is master of yours. What can change is how much the fear rules you. A person ruled by the fear of death can be pushed into almost anything. Someone who has made some peace with it has one less chain. Seneca isn't asking anyone to stop loving their life, or to be careless with it. Listeners bring their own beliefs about what comes after death, and the letter doesn't argue with any of them. He's asking something smaller: that we look at the fear in daylight instead of letting it work in the dark. A fear looked at in daylight is still there. It's just smaller, like the hallway with the light on.
screen: `A CHILD'S FEARS, GROWN UP.` · `CLINGING TO THE BRAMBLES.` · `ANYONE CAN TAKE A LIFE.` · `NAME THE FEAR IN DAYLIGHT.` · then, large: `FACE IT.`

segments.voice: If this topic is heavy for you today, simply rest with your breath instead. Otherwise, think of one fear you carry, about death or anything, and say it plainly in one short sentence, without arguing or fixing. Let it stand in the light, and notice you're still here, breathing, with the fear named.
Mors. Latin for death: Seneca's fourth letter, clinging to life like brambles in a flood keeps us from living, and facing the fear in daylight makes us freer.
Your line: face it. Looking at a fear isn't the same as being ruled by it. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Stoics practice reflecting calmly on death, not to dwell on it, but so that fear of it has less hold over how they live day to day.
